strengths: MultiSPA is a valuable data and benchmark contribution: over 27M QA pairs from annotated real-world scenes cover depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size, with multiple referencing and answer formats. The contribution is primarily the dataset and its construction pipeline rather than architectural novelty.

The central empirical result is strong. In Table 2, fine-tuning InternVL2-8B improves average accuracy from 20.43% to 56.11%, with gains across every reported task group. Scene/scenario-disjoint evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond memorizing training images.

External transfer supports the usefulness of the learned capabilities. On BLINK, average accuracy increases from 57.9% to 84.3%, including visual correspondence from 39.0% to 89.5% and multi-view reasoning from 49.6% to 94.7%. These results substantially strengthen the case beyond evaluation on the authors' generated benchmark.

The pipeline includes thoughtful mechanisms for balancing viewpoint overlap and motion magnitude, sampling distinct motion groups, and selecting complementary object views. The paper provides equations, illustrative examples, algorithm snippets, and major training settings.

Table 4 shows that substantial spatial gains coexist with largely preserved general VQA performance. Together with the data/model scaling results, this supports a weak acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The evidence establishes two-image spatial task improvement more strongly than general multi-frame reasoning. Appendix F restricts even object-size inputs to two images, and there are no single-view, duplicated-view, or shuffled-view controls to quantify reliance on cross-view information rather than scene and object priors. External evaluation also does not establish quantitative motion accuracy across new domains.

Annotation correctness needs stronger validation. Equation (3) uses the strict condition 0 < projected depth < measured depth, which excludes exact surface agreement and lacks an explicit tolerance for reconstruction/sensor error. Listing 2 also does not fully enforce the claimed minimal-set property: it can return a pair when its second image alone already covers the target dimension. These are concrete concerns about the stated pipeline, although the manuscript does not establish their actual frequency in the generated data.

The quantitative evaluation obscures practical error severity. A single 20% relative-error threshold provides no continuous error distributions and becomes exact-match evaluation for zero displacement. Camera-vector and object-vector accuracy remain only 18.00% and 12.92%, respectively. Comparisons with relevant specialist geometric methods or tool-assisted baselines would better contextualize the utility of these predictions.

The auxiliary scientific claims are less securely established. Table 5 increases total training data from 500K to 3M or from 400K to 800K, so it does not isolate task diversity from additional training exposure. Table 6's three model configurations and hard-training/easy-testing setup do not distinguish emergence from optimization or capacity effects; hard-set test performance and repeated runs are absent.

The robotics evidence is an illustrative demonstration rather than a validated reward-annotation application. Figure 5 contains a short sequence and a static-object example, without aggregate errors, reward-ranking evaluation, or downstream policy learning. It supports potential usefulness but not reliable robotic deployment.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful implementation details. Exact scene/scenario split identifiers, the task composition and sampling procedure for the 3M training subset, and full baseline prompting/GPT-4 answer-normalization procedures are not supplied. The appendix refers to a website for complete templates, but the provided manuscript has a blank project-page field.

strengths: MultiSPA is a useful data and benchmark contribution: over 27M QA pairs spanning five spatial task families, with point, coordinate, and semantic references and both qualitative and quantitative outputs. Reusing annotated 3D/4D datasets provides a principled basis for scalable supervision. The main originality lies in this resource and its construction, rather than the standard LoRA training method.

The main empirical gains are substantial. Table 2 reports 56.11% average accuracy versus 20.43% for the base model, with improvements across every reported task group. Holding out scenes or scenarios strengthens the evidence beyond memorization of training images.

External evaluation provides meaningful support for transfer: BLINK average accuracy increases from 57.9% to 84.3%, including visual correspondence from 39.0% to 89.5% and multi-view reasoning from 49.6% to 94.7% (Table 3). These results make the contribution more convincing than evaluation solely on the authors’ benchmark.

The paper provides useful scaling experiments, checks retention of general VQA capabilities, and documents data-generation algorithms in the appendix. Overall, the demonstrated resource value and transfer gains favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate how much improvement requires integrating both frames. There are no single-frame, duplicated-frame, or shuffled-pair controls, particularly for object size and metric estimation where semantic priors can help. Comparisons are also restricted to general-purpose MLLMs; spatially specialized models or task-specific geometric systems would better contextualize the contribution.

Annotation quality is insufficiently validated for a paper centered on high-quality supervision. Equation 3 uses a strict projected-depth inequality without a stated tolerance or consistency check, making visibility sensitive to reconstruction and sensor discrepancies. Listing 2 also does not fully enforce the claimed minimal-set property: it can return a pair containing a later-indexed image that already covers the dimension alone. The listing is explicitly simplified, so this does not establish that the actual dataset is incorrect, but the manuscript lacks an annotation audit to resolve these concerns.

Quantitative accuracy remains limited: camera and object displacement-vector accuracies are 18.00% and 12.92%, respectively. The fixed 20% relative-error criterion provides little insight into error magnitude and becomes especially stringent near zero displacement. Continuous errors and threshold curves would clarify practical usefulness. Figure 5 offers an illustrative robotics example, not a quantitative validation of reward annotation.

The auxiliary interpretations exceed the experimental controls. Table 5 increases total training data when adding tasks, leaving task diversity confounded with training volume and compute. Table 6 compares three model configurations and evaluates hard-trained models on easy examples; without repeated runs or optimization controls, the result supports capacity-dependent learning more clearly than emergent spatial ability.

Reproducibility is partial. Although several training settings and algorithm snippets are provided, exact scene/sequence splits, the task composition of the 3M-sample training subset, complete templates, and baseline prompting/post-processing details are not supplied in the manuscript. The appendix directs readers to a website for templates, but the project-page field is blank. These are correctable reporting gaps, distinct from the material evidential limitations above.

strengths: The principal contribution is a useful data resource for multi-view spatial understanding: 27M QA pairs from 1.1M images, covering depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and size with diverse referencing and output formats. Using existing 3D/4D annotations provides a principled basis for scalable supervision.

The empirical gains are substantial. On the scene/scenario-disjoint MultiSPA benchmark, the fine-tuned 8B model improves average accuracy from 20.43% to 56.11% (Table 2), with improvements across all reported task groups. The unchanged architecture makes the contribution of spatial supervision particularly clear.

External evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond the authors' benchmark. On four BLINK subsets, average accuracy rises from 57.9% to 84.3%, including visual correspondence from 39.0% to 89.5% and multi-view reasoning from 49.6% to 94.7% (Table 3). Standard VQA results show mostly modest changes rather than catastrophic forgetting.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful generation algorithms, training settings, scaling experiments, and explicit limitations. Taken together, the dataset contribution and strong external transfer support weak acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not fully establish how much performance requires integrating views rather than exploiting learned priors. There are no single-view or shuffled-pair controls, particularly relevant for metric size estimation. Comparisons primarily use general-purpose MLLMs; the absence of specialized spatial or geometry-based baselines limits conclusions about the approach's comparative advantages.

The multi-task experiments do not isolate task diversity from additional training volume and computation. Table 5 compares 500K camera-motion examples against 3M mixed examples, and 400K object-motion examples against 800K mixed examples. These demonstrate benefits from adding auxiliary data, but not an independent advantage over compute-matched single-task training.

Annotation correctness and reproducibility need stronger support. Equation (3) uses a strict depth inequality that excludes exact surface agreement and does not specify a tolerance for reconstruction noise. No quantitative annotation audit is reported. Exact scene splits, the composition of the selected 3M training examples, and complete templates are also insufficiently specified; the appendix refers to a website while the project-page field is blank.

The thresholded accuracy metric obscures geometric error distributions: a 20% relative tolerance becomes zero at zero displacement and very stringent near zero. Absolute-error statistics and threshold sensitivity would clarify practical precision. This matters because camera-vector and object-vector accuracies remain only 18.00% and 12.92%, respectively, and external quantitative motion generalization is not systematically evaluated.

The broader claims should remain narrower than the demonstrated results. Experiments use at most two views; the robotics reward-annotation example lacks downstream policy evaluation or aggregate statistics. Likewise, hard-to-easy correspondence results for three differently configured model sizes do not distinguish emergent capability from optimization or representation differences. These limitations temper the secondary claims without negating the central dataset and transfer contribution.

strengths: The principal contribution is a useful data-generation framework and large-scale dataset for spatial understanding across image pairs. Combining annotated geometry and motion from ScanNet, ADT, and Panoptic Studio supports substantially richer supervision than single-image spatial QA, including correspondences and camera/object displacement vectors.

The main empirical improvements are substantial: Table 2 reports 56.11% average accuracy versus 20.43% for the base model and 30.31% for the strongest proprietary baseline. Gains span qualitative and quantitative tasks, and the benchmark explicitly separates training and evaluation scenes or scenarios.

External evaluation provides convincing evidence that improvements extend beyond the generated benchmark. On four spatial subsets of BLINK, average accuracy increases from 57.9% to 84.3%, including visual correspondence from 39.0% to 89.5% and multi-view reasoning from 49.6% to 94.7%. Additional CVBench-3D and ERQA results strengthen this evidence, although their gains are smaller.

The experiments usefully investigate data scaling, model capacity, trainable components, and cross-task transfer. Table 8 particularly demonstrates that training the visual encoder materially improves geometric prediction. General VQA evaluations also indicate that most original capabilities are retained.

The manuscript explains the pipeline clearly and supplies algorithms, templates, examples, and substantial supplementary evaluation. Overall, the supported dataset and empirical contribution favor acceptance despite reservations about annotation validation and some broader interpretations.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is insufficiently validated for a dataset-centered contribution. Equation (3) defines visibility using the strict inequality z < D(u,v), which excludes exact surface agreement and lacks a tolerance for reconstruction/sensor discrepancies. No quantitative annotation audit establishes the effect on correspondences and overlap estimates. Additionally, Listing 2 does not enforce minimality against every proper subset: a pair can be retained even when its second image alone satisfies coverage. These issues leave uncertainty about the advertised label quality and requirement to integrate both views.

The multi-task experiments support beneficial auxiliary training but do not isolate task diversity from additional training volume and optimization. For example, Table 5 compares 500K target-task samples with 3M mixed samples, and 400K object-motion samples with 800K mixed samples. Tables 12–13 provide useful additional evidence, but lack matched-budget target-task or unrelated-data controls.

The expert-model comparison is difficult to interpret consistently. The main text describes approximately 72% camera-vector accuracy as matching VGGT, whereas Table 9 reports 86% versus 82% after scale normalization. The normalization procedure is not specified sufficiently, and the comparison uses different specialized model variants across tasks. It therefore does not establish that the default general-purpose model matches experts on metric geometric prediction.

Some broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Table 6 tests only three model configurations and one hard-to-easy training setup, which cannot distinguish emergence from optimization or capacity effects. Table 14 shows robustness to inserted intermediate frames, but does not demonstrate that those frames contribute information. The robotics reward-annotation example is illustrative rather than a quantitative downstream validation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix: exact scene/sequence split identifiers, the composition and selection of the 3M training subset, and the baseline prompting/post-processing protocol are not fully specified. The evaluation also lacks continuous geometric errors or threshold-sensitivity results; its 20% relative-error criterion becomes particularly restrictive near zero motion. These omissions limit interpretation of the low default camera-vector and object-vector accuracies of 18.00% and 12.92%, respectively.

strengths: The main contribution is a useful data resource for multi-frame spatial perception: over 27M QA samples, five task families, multiple referencing methods, and quantitative outputs including coordinates and displacement vectors. Constructing these from annotated 3D/4D datasets provides substantial value beyond the conventional fine-tuning method.

The principal empirical result is strong. On the scene/scenario-disjoint MultiSPA benchmark, the 8B model improves from 20.43% to 56.11% average accuracy (Table 2), with gains across every reported category. Correspondence MCQ accuracy reaches 90%, and quantitative correspondence improves from 1.67% to 49%.

External evaluation supports transfer beyond the generated benchmark. On the four evaluated BLINK subsets, average accuracy rises from 57.9% to 84.3%, including 94.7% on multi-view reasoning (Table 3). Supplementary evaluations also show gains on CVBench-3D and ERQA's multi-frame subset, although overall ERQA improvement is small.

The supplementary experiments materially strengthen the submission. Table 8 tests several tuning strategies, Tables 12–13 investigate cross-task transfer, and Figure 4 demonstrates scaling on camera-vector prediction. General VQA evaluations indicate that most original capabilities are retained, with some modest declines.

Overall, the demonstrated dataset utility and substantial external transfer provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection. The reservations concern annotation verification, experimental attribution, and broader claims; they do not erase the supported contribution.
weaknesses: The annotation pipeline has an unresolved technical concern. Equation 3 defines visibility using the strict inequality 0 < z < D(u,v). As written, this excludes points exactly on the measured surface and does not require agreement with that surface within a tolerance. Reconstruction and depth noise could therefore affect correspondence labels and overlap estimates. No quantitative annotation-quality audit establishes the impact; this is a substantive uncertainty for a dataset-centered paper, although it does not establish that the implementation is incorrect.

The evaluation does not fully isolate learning to integrate multiple views from learning dataset priors. There are no single-frame or shuffled-pair controls, particularly relevant to metric depth, object size, and motion magnitude. RGB inputs alone do not uniquely determine absolute metric scale. Appendix L shows robustness when intermediate frames are added, but a model using only the endpoints could obtain the same result; it does not establish integration of the additional views.

The closest methodological comparison is incomplete. SAT is discussed as concurrent multi-frame spatial training, but is not compared experimentally. SpatialRGPT's poor performance is insufficient to conclude that single-image supervision generally fails to transfer, since model architecture, data distribution, and referencing conventions also differ. The originality is primarily in the resource and task coverage rather than the learning algorithm.

The expert-model comparison needs clearer qualification. Table 9 uses scale-normalized camera vectors and reports VGGT versus the proposed model as 86 versus 82, whereas the main text emphasizes approximately 72% metric-vector accuracy. These measure different properties. The normalization procedure and expert-task protocols are insufficiently specified, and the general-capability retention results do not establish retention for the separately trained, fully fine-tuned expert-comparison variants.

The stronger interpretive claims exceed the experiments. Multi-task comparisons add training data and optimization steps, without matched-budget controls separating these effects from task diversity. The emergence study uses three model configurations, evaluates hard-trained models on easy examples, and reports neither repeated runs nor optimization diagnostics. It supports capacity-dependent learnability, but does not distinguish emergence from optimization or representation limitations. The robotics examples illustrate possible reward annotation rather than demonstrate its usefulness for learning a policy.

Reproducibility is partial despite helpful pseudocode and training hyperparameters. The exact scene/sequence split identifiers, full composition of the 3M training subset, complete templates, and baseline post-processing prompts are not supplied. Thresholded accuracy also obscures error magnitude and becomes exact-match scoring for zero displacement; continuous errors and near-zero-motion breakdowns would make practical performance easier to assess, especially given the main model's 18% camera-vector and 12.92% object-vector accuracy.

strengths: The principal contribution is a useful, substantial dataset and benchmark for multi-frame spatial perception. MultiSPA combines annotated 3D/4D sources with diverse referencing and answer formats across 26 subtasks. Overlap-balanced sampling, motion-based sampling, and object-coverage selection are thoughtful components beyond simply templating existing annotations.

The central empirical result is convincing: the 8B model improves MultiSPA accuracy from 20.43% to 56.11% (Table 2), with gains across all reported task groups. Evaluation scenes are held out from training. Table 8 further demonstrates that the data supports stronger results when the vision encoder and additional parameters are trained.

External evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond the authors' benchmark. BLINK performance rises from 57.9% to 84.3%, including substantial improvements in visual correspondence and multi-view reasoning. The appendix adds positive results on CVBench-3D and ERQA, although their gains are smaller.

The approach retains the existing MLLM architecture and largely preserves general VQA performance. Training settings, data-generation algorithms, templates, and additional ablations are documented. Overall, the supported dataset contribution and transferable gains favor acceptance despite reservations about some secondary claims.
weaknesses: The evidence for task synergy does not fully separate task diversity from additional training data and optimization. Table 5 compares 500K versus 3M examples and 400K versus 800K examples. Tables 12–13 strengthen the transfer evidence but still lack matched-budget target-only or repeated-data controls. These experiments support beneficial auxiliary supervision more directly than an independent task-diversity scaling effect.

The expert-model comparison needs a more precise evaluation protocol. Appendix I introduces scale normalization without specifying how the scale is obtained or applied to each method. Table 9 reports VGGT versus the proposed model as 86 versus 82, whereas the main text discusses approximately 72% camera-vector accuracy. These appear to involve different evaluation conditions and cannot directly establish parity in metric translation estimation. The configurations also differ from the primary LoRA model evaluated for general VQA retention.

The emergence claim is preliminary. Table 6 contains only three model configurations, changes encoder and language-model capacity, and provides no repeated runs or optimization controls. Failure of smaller models to learn from hard distractors could reflect training difficulty rather than an emergent spatial ability. The authors acknowledge uncertainty, but the abstract and conclusion give this observation more prominence than the evidence warrants.

Practical multi-frame capability remains narrower than some framing suggests. Training uses image pairs, and inserting intermediate frames while querying the first-to-last motion (Table 14) demonstrates robustness but does not establish integration of additional views. The main model achieves only 18.00% camera-vector and 12.92% object-vector accuracy. Robotics reward annotation is illustrated qualitatively, without reward-quality statistics or downstream learning results.

Some benchmark and data-generation details limit reproducibility and interpretation. Equation 3 uses a strict depth inequality without explaining tolerance or handling reconstruction noise; Appendix E gives absolute yaw/pitch formulas without explicitly specifying relative-angle wrapping. Baseline outputs undergo GPT-4 post-processing without a documented audit of answer preservation. Finally, thresholded accuracy alone obscures numerical error severity, especially near zero motion, where the relative-error tolerance collapses.
